title: Organising Bigger Programs
summary: Break a longer program into named scenes — each scene is its own function.

content.title: Programs Get Long
content.summary: As programs grow, it becomes hard to find things. Functions are the solution: one function, one job.
content.body:
When programs get long, they get hard to read. You scroll up and down trying to remember where things happen.

Functions solve this by giving every section a name:

• intro() — the opening
• choose_path() — the decision
• battle() — the fight
• ending() — the finale

Now the program reads like a list of chapters.

content.title: A Program Made of Scenes
content.summary: Define one function per scene. At the bottom, call them in story order.
content.body:
def intro():
    print("Welcome to the dungeon.")
    print("A dark passage lies ahead.")

def battle():
    print("A skeleton rattles towards you!")
    print("You raise your shield.")
    print("Victory!")

def ending():
    print("You escape the dungeon.")
    print("The sun feels warm.")

intro()
battle()
ending()

At the very bottom, three lines tell the whole story.

content.title: One Function, One Job
content.summary: Each function should do exactly one thing. If a function does three unrelated things, split it.
content.body:
A good rule: each function should do one clear job.

If battle() also prints the shop inventory and the ending message, it is doing too much.

Break it apart:
• battle() — just the fight
• show_shop() — just the shop
• ending() — just the finale

Smaller functions are easier to fix, easier to test, and easier to reuse.

content.title: Reading the Program at a Glance
content.summary: The bottom of the file should read like a story outline — just function calls in order.
content.body:
When your program is well-organised, the bottom few lines tell the whole story:

intro()
choose_weapon()
battle()
level_up()
ending()

Anyone reading this knows exactly what happens, in what order, without reading a single detail. That is good code design.

editorPrompt: Build a 3-scene mini story: write intro(), middle(), and ending() functions, each with 2–3 print lines. Call all three at the bottom in order.
starterCode:
# A mini story in three scenes
def intro():
    pass

def middle():
    pass

def ending():
    pass

# Tell the story
intro()
middle()
ending()
progressiveHints: Replace each pass with 2–3 print lines that fit that scene of the story.
Keep each function focused on just its scene — don't put battle details in intro().
The three calls at the bottom are already there — just make sure your functions are filled in.
Bonus: give your middle() function a parameter, like middle(enemy), and pass a monster name when you call it.
challenge: Add a fourth function called plot_twist() with a surprise reveal. Insert it between middle() and ending() in the story calls at the bottom.
